strengths: Novel and creative application of LLMs to computational conlanging, testing metalinguistic reasoning on out-of-distribution tasks
Linguistically-informed decomposition into phonology, morphology, syntax, and lexicon with appropriate sequential generation
Thoughtful methodology combining randomness injection for diversity and self-refinement for consistency
Comprehensive evaluation framework with automatic metrics, ablation study, and manual validation attempt
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and diverse qualitative examples demonstrating user control
Interesting constructive translation framing allowing dynamic expansion of language descriptions
weaknesses: Severely limited scale with only ~20 languages, 10 test sentences per language, and critically, only 1 human annotator without inter-annotator agreement—insufficient for strong empirical claims
Modest absolute performance (consistency rates 0.35-0.44) directly contradicts claims that the system produces 'coherent and varied conlangs'
Weak baseline (naive single-stage prompt) with no comparison to existing conlanging tools, other decompositions, or human-created languages—cannot assess practical meaningfulness of improvements

LLM-as-judge evaluation for consistency against potentially underspecified grammars is of questionable reliability; moderate agreement with manual evaluation (ρ=0.515) suggests they measure different constructs
Typological diversity metric (Hamming distance over WALS features) is shallow and only measures feature differences, not linguistic coherence or true novelty
Insufficient linguistic validation with cherry-picked examples and no systematic error analysis; unclear whether creative outputs actually work operationally
Constructive translation allowing dynamic grammar addition during evaluation complicates interpretation of consistency scores
Unclear practical utility—no evidence that actual conlangers would find outputs useful at 35-44% consistency, and claims about low-resource language applications appear tenuous
Methodological details missing (self-refinement iteration statistics, computational costs, rejection sampling rates) and results vary significantly across model variants
Individual technical components are not novel; contributions are primarily in application domain

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First end-to-end computational conlang generation system; creative framing of generation as multi-hop reasoning
Linguistically-motivated architecture: Decomposition into phonology→grammar→lexicon parallels linguistic theory and multi-hop reasoning approaches
Comprehensive system design: Thoughtful integration of randomness injection for diversity, self-refinement for consistency, and optional user control
Qualitative richness: Impressive diverse outputs (Tables 4-5) demonstrating grasp of typological variation, including creative/unusual features
Evaluation framework development: Proposes metrics for typological diversity and consistency with attempt at validation against manual judgment
weaknesses: Limited relevance to ACL: Addresses constructed languages (fictional, artificial) rather than natural language processing. Speculative applications to low-resource languages and video game design are outside core NLP scope and remain unvalidated

Critically weak evaluation: (1) Circular evaluation using LLMs to judge LLM outputs; (2) Only 1 human annotator from authors' institution on 200 data points with no inter-rater reliability; (3) Moderate agreement (ρ=0.515, κ=0.304) poorly validates automatic metrics; (4) Automatic metrics acknowledged as 'stricter than manual' suggesting miscalibration

Poor absolute performance: Consistency rates of 35-44% mean translations violate language rules in 56-65% of cases, severely undermining the core goal. Troubling pattern in Table 3: randomness injection *decreases* consistency (0.40→0.27), with only partial recovery via self-refinement

Extremely limited experimental scope: Fixed 10 test sentences for all evaluations; ~20 languages with unexplained rejection sampling (N=15-21); short language descriptions acknowledged as insufficient; no diverse translation stress-testing

Insufficient baselines and ablations: Only single-stage baseline (no comparison to multi-prompt alternatives, improved prompting, or other decomposition strategies); missing ablations on WALS feature selection, refinement iteration limits, prompt sensitivity

Limited methodological novelty: Multi-hop decomposition (standard), randomness injection (straightforward), self-refinement (applies existing techniques). Novelty is primarily in application domain, not methods

Reproducibility concerns: Hyperparameters listed as 'default' without specification; computational costs unreported; full prompts relegated to repository; code not provided; different LLM variants show inconsistent performance
Insufficient error analysis: No investigation of common error types, typological combinations that fail, or explanation for large consistency drops. No qualitative failure case analysis
Arbitrary design choices: Why 10 typological features with 5 options? Why these 16 specific WALS features? Why these 10 test sentences? No sensitivity analysis or justification

Scalability limitations: Acknowledged incompatibility with larger grammars/lexicons due to context windows—not merely future work but fundamental constraint. Short language summaries 'too short to capture a fraction of real language complexity'

Coarse evaluation metrics: Binary consistency metric (acknowledged but unaddressed). Diversity measured on only 16 WALS features—reductive for capturing true cross-linguistic variation. No validation that metric improvements correlate with linguistic quality

strengths: Novel research direction: First work on end-to-end computational conlanging with LLMs, opening a genuine new area
Linguistically principled design: Decomposition into phonology-grammar-lexicon reflects sound linguistic theory; RNG injection for typological diversity is well-motivated

Comprehensive evaluation framework: Despite limitations, the paper thoughtfully develops automatic metrics (WALS-based diversity, consistency via translation) and validates against manual expert annotation
Strong ablation study: Table 3 clearly demonstrates contribution of each component (MH, RNG, SR) with interpretable trade-offs
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written paper with effective figures; full prompts in appendix; code repository promised
Credible validation: Manual evaluation by linguistics expert shows reasonable agreement with automatic metrics (ρ = 0.515, p < 10⁻¹⁴), supporting framework validity
Qualitative examples: Tables 4-5 demonstrate genuine linguistic diversity and creative language generation, including typologically unusual features
Thoughtful methodology: External RNG for diversity control and self-refinement with critic-editor paradigm are well-justified design choices
weaknesses: Critical evaluation limitation: Only one annotator for manual evaluation with no inter-annotator agreement; standard NLP practice requires 2-3 independent annotators, limiting validity of evaluation framework claims
Modest core results: Consistency rates of 35-44% indicate substantial remaining logical errors; paper inadequately discusses whether this is acceptable for practical use or what error types persist
Small sample size: N ≈ 20 languages limits statistical confidence and generalizability; confidence intervals reflect sampling rather than robustness
Weak baseline: Naive single-stage generation is reasonable given no prior work, but provides limited evidence that the decomposition strategy is optimal; alternative decompositions not compared
Limited scope of evaluation: Only 16 WALS features (of 200+) used; language sketches acknowledged as 'extremely short'; 10 test sentences per language; extremely limited token budget

Evaluation framework validity concerns: Binary consistency metric lacks granularity; moderate automatic-manual agreement (κ = 0.304) and strictness gap suggest misalignment; single LLM judge for validation
Constructive translation under-validated: Novel concept but limited systematic evaluation of whether new lexical/grammar additions are linguistically sensible or just plausible hallucinations
RNG mechanism not fully justified: Ablation shows MH alone achieves diversity 0.52; RNG adds only 0.08 more—is this substantial? No analysis of linguistic sensibility of RNG selections
Unresolved scalability concerns: Context-window limitations prevent realistic language sketches; acknowledged as fundamental but unresolved
Limited analysis of user control: Table 5 shows cherry-picked examples; no systematic evaluation of constraint adherence or violation rates

strengths: Novel research direction opening computational conlanging as a new field; first systematic end-to-end approach to LLM-based language generation
Well-motivated multi-hop methodology grounded in linguistic principles (phonology→grammar→lexicon decomposition mirrors language documentation practices)
Excellent reproducibility: complete prompts, language sketches, and implementation details provided; designed for verification and extension
Sophisticated evaluation framework with novel automatic metrics (WALS-based diversity, judge-based consistency) validated against manual expert annotation (ρ=0.68, κ=0.58)
Strong empirical results on diversity: 0.56-0.60 vs. baseline 0.25-0.35 (p<10⁻⁶, d>3.0) and natural languages (0.43), with compelling qualitative examples of typologically unusual combinations
Clever technical innovation: RNG-based randomness injection achieves high diversity (0.60) without consistency penalty of temperature sampling (which requires T=1.4 and crashes to 0.34)
Rigorous ablation study (Table 2) demonstrating cumulative contribution of multi-hop reasoning, randomness injection, and self-refinement
Thoughtful design of constructive translation framework addressing underspecification inherent to novel languages
weaknesses: Translation consistency only 38-54% despite claims of 'logical consistency'; no error analysis of failure modes (harmony violations, word order errors, phonotactic violations); diversity-consistency tradeoff suggests fundamental tension
Limited scale of evaluation: manual evaluation on only N=20 languages with 10 translations each; inter-annotator agreement κ=0.43 is moderate; automatic metrics on ~20 languages (varying N=17-21)

Insufficient validation of core research questions: RQ1 (languages 'distinct from training') not empirically verified; no evidence they avoid memorization vs. subtle recombination of training patterns

Evaluation metric limitations: WALS feature extraction has 12% underspecification and 4% false positives; 16-feature metric may miss typological novelty; binary consistency metric doesn't reflect violation severity; LLM-as-judge has known biases despite using external model

Weak representation of language structure: Sketches omit semantics, pragmatics, discourse, orthography; context length limits to ~100 lexical items; brief grammars cannot capture real-language complexity

Limited relevance to NLP/computational linguistics: work is more about LLM creative capabilities than advancing language understanding; speculative applications (game design, low-resource languages) underdeveloped
Significant computational cost (660K tokens ≈ $4 per language, largely self-refinement) with unclear practical value; not scalable for serious applications

Methodological gaps: checklist-based randomness (10 features × 5 options) may limit true diversity space; no analysis of feature coverage; multi-hop pipeline risks error compounding; rejection sampling not detailed
Generalization concerns: only 3 LLM configurations tested with substantial variance; small sample sizes (N≈20) limit statistical generalizability; results may not hold for future models

Limited error analysis and ablations: no breakdown of which languages/phenomena fail; no qualitative analysis of common inconsistencies; missing analysis of how often new lexical items violate phonotactics or grammar rules contradict existing rules

strengths: Novel application domain of computational conlanging with clear research questions
Thoughtful multi-hop pipeline architecture linguistically motivated and well-designed
Clever randomness injection via RNG that outperforms temperature-based diversity approaches
Comprehensive evaluation effort including automatic metrics, manual expert evaluation, and ablation studies
High reproducibility with detailed prompts, implementation details, and promised code release
Compelling qualitative examples demonstrating realistic linguistic features in generated languages
weaknesses: Weak empirical results: consistency of 0.54 in best case means ~46% of translations violate the language's own rules, undermining core claims of coherence
Limited technical novelty: multi-hop reasoning, self-refinement, and LLM-as-judge are established techniques; only randomness injection via RNG is novel but relatively straightforward

Evaluation methodology concerns: small scale (N≈20 languages, 2 annotators), moderate inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.43), LLM-as-judge validity unvalidated, crude metrics (binary consistency, Hamming distance for diversity)
WALS feature extraction errors: 12% of features left unspecified, 4% incorrectly inferred, undermining diversity metric reliability
Questionable claim of out-of-distribution reasoning: training data includes extensive conlang knowledge (Tolkien, etc.), contradicting the novelty argument
Unsubstantiated claim that exceeding natural language diversity is desirable without validating typological plausibility of extreme feature combinations
Problem design issue: constructive translation permits arbitrary invention of words/grammar rules, making it unclear how constrained the task actually is
No validation of practical utility: no user study with conlangers, no comparison to human-generated or existing conlangs, no evidence actual conlangers would find this useful
Limited scope: only covers phonology/morpho-syntax/lexicon; acknowledges language sketches too short to capture real language complexity
Missing error analysis: no investigation of which sentence types/grammatical phenomena cause low consistency; no justification for why consistency plateaus at 0.54
Weak baseline: single prompt without structure; no comparison to alternative structured approaches
Reproducibility concerns: depends on proprietary closed-weight models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1); results may not generalize or reproduce with model updates
Minimal engagement with conlanging literature, community tools, or what linguists/conlangers value in constructed languages

strengths: Novel and well-motivated application of LLMs to computational conlanging, testing metalinguistic reasoning on inherently out-of-distribution languages
Sound methodology combining multi-hop reasoning, randomness injection via typological checklists, and self-refinement loops grounded in linguistic theory
Thoughtful evaluation framework for creative tasks with no ground truth, validated against manual expert judgment (ρ=0.68)
Strong empirical results with large effect sizes (d>3.0 for diversity, p<10⁻⁶) and clear ablation study showing each component's contribution
Comprehensive reproducibility resources including full prompts, language sketches, implementation details, and thorough appendices
Honest treatment of limitations and transparent discussion of methodological tradeoffs
Clear practical applications to world-building, linguistic hypothesis testing, and hobbyist conlanging
weaknesses: Consistency performance remains modest (0.54 best case), contradicting core claim that method produces 'coherent' and 'internally consistent' languages; ~46% of translations fail consistency check
Limited evaluation scale (N≈20 languages, 10 sentences each, 2 manual annotators) limits confidence in generalizations, though pragmatically justified
Diversity metric narrowly scoped to 16 of ~200+ WALS features; claim of exceeding natural language diversity (0.60 vs 0.43) may not reflect overall linguistic diversity
Automatic consistency metric is binary (fully consistent or not), losing information compared to ordinal manual scale (0-2); moderate inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.43)
Feature extraction has non-negligible error rate (12% unspecified, 4% incorrectly inferred); unclear what percentage of generated languages have all 16 WALS features specified
Language descriptions limited to three layers (phonology, morphology, syntax); omit semantics, pragmatics, orthography; constructive translation limited to 10 predefined sentences
Randomness injection method is somewhat ad-hoc (checklist + RNG) with limited justification versus alternatives; generalizability unclear
High computational cost (660K tokens/$4 per language, largely from self-refinement) limits reproducibility; modest consistency improvement may not justify 10x token increase
Limited error analysis: insufficient detail on what types of inconsistencies persist post-refinement, which linguistic phenomena cause most difficulty, or why self-refinement fails in 46% of cases
LLM-as-judge methodology has known biases and limitations; moderate agreement with human evaluation suggests automatic metrics may not fully capture linguistic quality
